e6c2558dd35f707f4d1cc8ec4285d49c74e612aa.summary: A 2015 TrendLabs blog post by Trend Micro senior threat researcher David Sancho describes how malware uses steganography to hide code and command-and-control (C&C) traffic. It cites a DarkComet dropper, seen in November 2014, that hides encrypted code in a bitmap image in its resources. It describes the Morto Trojan sending Base64-encoded C&C commands in DNS responses, the TDSS/Alureon botnet fetching JPG images from popular blogging sites with commands hidden inside, and ShadyRAT hiding commands in HTML comments and in JPG files using LSB encoding. e66c29589f2d77b18611624a8f1f7ac655ab133e.summary: Kaspersky ICS CERT describes SalmonSlalom, a campaign against government and industrial organisations in the Asia-Pacific region, mostly Chinese-speaking targets. Malicious archives sent by email, WeChat and Telegram start a long chain: loaders fetch configuration from Youdao Cloud Notes and a Chinese cloud CDN, abuse the legitimate PureCodec and DriverAssistant programs through DLL sideloading, and finally run the FatalRAT backdoor. The authors could not link it to a known group; a Chinese-speaking actor is assumed with medium confidence.

hedges: The authors could not link the activity to any known group; a Chinese-speaking actor is assumed with only medium confidence.
ESET does not attribute this activity to any known group, while TrendMicro linked FatalRAT to the Purple Fox botnet.
Weibu did not attribute its series to a named group and gave it the name Silver Fox.
Cofense notes technique similarity to APT27 but draws no conclusion about who was behind the activity.
Reusing the same IP address across campaigns is only speculated; the authors suspect it may be shared.
The file named in a commented-out script line is described as most likely part of the attack, but no other traces were found.
The Youdao note contents were updated regularly but were no longer active at the time of writing.
